leftCard.title: US Treasury Bonds
leftCard.subtitle: Actual / Actual (in period)
points: Counts exact actual calendar days between dates.
Divides by exact actual days in the semiannual coupon period (e.g. 181 or 184 days).
Accounts for leap years and exact calendar day differences.
Used for all US Treasury bonds and notes.

rightCard.title: Corporate & Municipal Bonds
rightCard.subtitle: 30 / 360 Convention
points: Assumes every full calendar month has exactly 30 days.
Assumes every year has exactly 360 days (12 months x 30 days).
Simplifies manual interest accounting for corporate issuers.
Used for US corporate bonds and municipal municipal debt.

data.contrast: Exact calendar days vs standardized 30-day months

semantics.teachingObjective: Contrast Treasury Actual/Actual rule against corporate 30/360 standard

subtitlePhrases.text: Three main day count conventions dominate fixed income: Actual/Actual,

beats.hindi_tts: Treasury bonds count exact calendar days. Corporate bonds assume each month contains 30 days and the year contains 360 days.
beats.en_subtitle: Treasury bonds count exact calendar days. Corporate bonds assume 30 days per month and 360 days per year.
beats.en_narration: Treasury bonds count exact calendar days. Corporate bonds assume each month contains 30 days and the year contains 360 days.

leftCard.title: Actual / Actual Ratio
leftCard.subtitle: Interest Fraction
points: Let d = actual days elapsed since last coupon.
Let D = actual days in current coupon period.
Accrued Interest = (Annual Coupon / 2) x (d / D).
Perfect mathematical reflection of true elapsed time.

rightCard.title: 30 / 360 Ratio
rightCard.subtitle: Interest Fraction
points: Day count formula: 360(Y2 - Y1) + 30(M2 - M1) + (D2 - D1).
Denominator is always 180 for semiannual coupons.
February 28th and 31-day months are adjusted by special rule sets.
Slightly diverges from exact solar calendar time.

beats.hindi_tts: Furthermore, money market instruments such as Treasury bills, repo, and commercial paper use Actual/360 convention.

leftCard.title: Actual / 360 Money Market
leftCard.subtitle: T-Bills, Repo, Commercial Paper
points: Counts exact actual elapsed calendar days.
Divides by 360-day year denominator.
Effectively increases the annualized interest rate by 365/360 (approx 1.39%).
Standard across international money markets and interbank deposits.

rightCard.title: Market Implications
rightCard.subtitle: Yield Comparison Caveat
points: Traders cannot directly compare T-bill discount rates to T-bond yields.
Must convert money market rates to bond-equivalent yield (BEY).
Prevents mispricing when constructing zero curves.

cards.title: 1. Contract Size & Delivery Basket
cards.subtitle: $100,000 Par Value · 15 to 25 Years to Maturity
cards.description: Each contract represents $100,000 face value of US Treasury bonds. The exchange permits delivery of any Treasury bond that has at least 15 years and less than 25 years to maturity (and not callable within 15 years).

cards.title: 2. Quotation in Thirty-Seconds
cards.subtitle: Points & 32nds (e.g., 90-16)
cards.description: Prices are quoted as percentage of par in points and 32nds. A quote of 90-16 means 90 + 16/32 = 90.50% of par ($90,500). One 32nd equals $31.25 per contract.

cards.title: 3. Delivery Window & Short's Discretion
cards.subtitle: Entire Delivery Month Available
cards.description: Delivery can occur on any business day of the delivery month. Crucially, the short position decides which bond to deliver and on which exact date to initiate delivery.

cards.title: 4. The Multi-Bond Dilemma
cards.subtitle: Dozens of Eligible Issues
cards.description: Because dozens of Treasury bonds meet the 15-25 year rule with different coupon rates, the exchange must standardize them to prevent arbitrage distortions.

leftCard.title: Market Yields > 6.0%
leftCard.subtitle: High Yield Regime
points: Conversion factor formula penalizes low-coupon, long-maturity bonds.
Market prices these bonds even lower than the CF assumes.
Long-maturity, low-coupon bonds become Cheapest-to-Deliver.
Duration of futures contract extends toward 20+ years.

rightCard.title: Market Yields < 6.0%
rightCard.subtitle: Low Yield Regime
points: Conversion factor formula rewards high-coupon, short-maturity bonds.
Short-maturity, high-coupon bonds become Cheapest-to-Deliver.
Duration of futures contract contracts toward 15 years.
Dominates during low-rate central bank easing cycles.

leftCard.title: Why Yields > 6% Favor Long
leftCard.subtitle: Mathematical Pricing Bias
points: Bonds yielding > 6% trade at a market discount.
The longer the maturity, the greater the price discount in the cash market.
CF formula does not fully reflect this discount, making spot cheaper to acquire.
Basis traders aggressively short the long bond basis.

rightCard.title: Portfolio Implication
rightCard.subtitle: Dynamic Duration Tracking
points: As yields rise above 6%, the futures contract behaves like a 25-year bond.
Portfolio managers must adjust hedge ratios to account for higher duration.
Failure to update CTD duration causes serious hedging mismatches.

leftCard.title: Yield Curve Slope Impact
leftCard.subtitle: Upward vs Inverted Curves
points: Upward sloping curve: Long yields > short yields, pushing CTD toward longer bonds.

points: Short party can switch CTD bonds mid-month if yields cross the 6% threshold.

ui_state.heading: The 8 Core Bond Futures Laws
steps: 1. Day Count Conventions: Treasuries use Actual/Actual, corporates use 30/360, and money markets use Actual/360.
2. Dirty Cash Price: Buyer pays Clean Quoted Price plus Accrued Interest: Cash = Clean + AI.
3. T-Bond Futures Basket: Contracts allow delivery of any Treasury bond maturing in 15 to 25 years.
4. Conversion Factors (CF): Equalize heterogeneous bonds to a 6.0% semiannual yield standard.
5. CTD Cost Formula: Short delivers the bond minimizing Cost = Spot Clean Price - (Futures * CF).
6. The 6% Yield Heuristic: Yields > 6% favor long-maturity low-coupon; yields < 6% favor short-maturity high-coupon.
7. The Wild Card Play: 6-hour delivery notice window post-2 PM allows shorts to profit from late price drops.
8. Embedded Option Value: Short delivery flexibility systematically lowers futures prices below cash parity.
ui_state.bottomTakeaway: Treasury bond futures pricing is governed by the cheapest-to-deliver bond, standardized via conversion factors.
